newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl hungry for fifth term after strict diet.
newsitem.headline: Kohl hungry for fifth term after strict diet.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl saves some of his most difficult decisions for his Easter dieting vacation in Austria, where the daily fare of bread rolls and water seems to whet his appetite for politics.

The 10 days of fasting and reflection in the Alps this year helped him come to the conclusion he announced on Thursday, his 67th birthday, that he would seek re-election for an unprecedented fifth term when the next general election comes around in late 1998.

Speaking in a television interview at the Austrian resort of Bad Hofgastein, Kohl said he wanted to stay on to help guide NATO's eastward expansion, Europe's integration and the launch of the European Union's planned single currency in 1999.
It was a bold move by the burly man who regularly upstages rivals who make the mistake of underestimating him.

With his enormous girth and slightly slurred speech, "The Fat Man" has long been a favourite target of jokes in Germany. But unbeaten in the polls in the last two decades, Kohl has always enjoyed the last laugh.
His decision to stand for re-election was in doubt until now because another Kohl trait -- his tendency to withdraw and delay any decisions -- had maintained the upper hand in recent months.

Fierce criticism over the country's growing economic woes and record unemployment have rained down on Kohl for months. Young leaders in his Christian Democratic (CDU) party have criticised him for weak leadership and his loyal lieutenant, Wolfgang Schaeuble, hinted he was ready to take over.
But Kohl thrives when the naysayers raise their collective voices. He enjoys striking back just when it seems he is on the ropes for the last time.
He has been there so often that the press has a word for it -- "Kanzlerdaemmerung" or "twilight of the chancellor".

Dubbed "the eternal chancellor" by the weekly magazine Der Spiegel, Kohl is Bonn's longest-serving chancellor. He has won four straight elections and served for 14-1/2 years, surpassing his mentor Konrad Adenauer's record in office last October.

If he wins re-election and serves the full four years, Kohl will have been chancellor for 20 years and beat the record set by Count Otto von Bismarck, the "Iron Chancellor" of the late 19th-century chancellor who served for 19 years and two months.
Kohl, who stands 1.93 metres (six feet four inches) tall and whose weight fluctuates around 115 kg (250 lb), has the political clout to match his towering physique.
As chancellor since 1982, Kohl has outlasted such political contemporaries as Ronald Reagan, Margaret Thatcher, Francois Mitterrand and Mikhail Gorbachev.
He is the only chancellor a generation of Germans has known and he dominates the political scene in Germany in a way that leaders in other western countries can only dream about.
He silenced critics from within his CDU last month with a thunderous put-down: "These idiots give interviews morning, noon and night."
Often deaf to his critics, Kohl openly snubs the country's leading newsweekly, Der Spiegel, and is notoriously choosy about which TV reporters he will let interview him.

A powerful figure in the European Union, Kohl is a tireless advocate for European integration. He is among the most vocal champions of the European economic and monetary union (EMU) and cited the project as key reason he wants to serve another term.

His word carries weight on issues like key appointments in the EU and his constant pressure on Paris has kept the Franco-German axis -- the motor of European integration -- stay on course after President Jacques Chirac seemed less interested than his predecessor Mitterrand in coordinating policy.
Many Eastern European countries eager to join the EU and NATO also see him as their best ally in the west.
Kohl enjoys close friendships with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, with whom has has shared a sauna, and a fellow big eater in Washington, U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Kohl used a soundbite from Clinton in his last election campaign that showed the president saying he always looked to see how Helmut was voting before making up his mind.
Kohl's place in history has already been secured with his widely applauded efforts in reuniting Germany in 1990.
He first ran for chancellor in 1976, narrowly losing to Helmut Schmidt. Then he stood aside as the right's best orator, Franz Josef Strauss, ran but lost in 1980.
Kohl finally made it in 1982 when the small Free Democratic Party (FDP) deserted Schmidt and formed a government with him.
Kohl, the Roman Catholic son of a minor civil servant, was born on April 3, 1930, in the Rhine river port of Ludwigshafen. The end of World War Two found him in an army cadet school.

He won a doctorate in history at Heidelberg University and was the youngest member of the Rhineland-Palatinate state assembly when he entered it in 1959. A decade later, he was the state premier and on his way to the top.
He has a wife, Hannelore, and two grown-up sons.
